title: Flu Season 2

jokes.text: Martin's audition: playing Quentin Tarantino casting John Malkovich, then adding Tommy Lee Jones who hates movies, then George W. Bush
jokes.setup: Auditions for the local talent stage of the Unity Concert — we expect performers doing actual acts
jokes.punchline: Martin performs a bizarre multi-celebrity impersonation skit involving Tarantino, Malkovich, Tommy Lee Jones (who hates movies), and George W. Bush with no apparent logic
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity of the celebrity mashup is funny — Tommy Lee Jones declaring 'I hate movies' is the best beat. The George W. Bush non-sequitur caps it well. Moderately original but not tightly structured.

dialogue.speaker: Martin
dialogue.line: I'm gonna do impressions of celebrities for the Unity Concert talent show.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Interviewer
dialogue.line: Oh great, what impressions do you do?

dialogue.speaker: Martin
dialogue.line: *does completely nonsensical mashup of random celebrity impressions that makes no sense*

jokes.text: Leslie's reaction: 'Who are any of those people?' — delivered flatly to camera as if she couldn't parse any of the celebrities
jokes.setup: Martin just performed a multi-celebrity impersonation skit
jokes.punchline: Leslie, a hyper-competent overachiever, has apparently never heard of Quentin Tarantino, John Malkovich, or Tommy Lee Jones
jokes.explanation: Short, economical, and true to Leslie's character — she is laser-focused on tasks and pop culture outside her wheelhouse doesn't register. The deadpan delivery makes it land. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Interviewer
dialogue.line: Those were impressive impressions, but what was the point?

dialogue.speaker: Martin
dialogue.line: The point? There is no point. I just do voices.

jokes.text: Perd Hapley: 'This is a slam poem that I wrote. And I am speaking the slam poem to you right now with my mouth.'
jokes.setup: Perd Hapley announces he will perform a slam poem as his audition
jokes.punchline: He narrates what he is doing with maximum redundancy — 'speaking the slam poem to you right now with my mouth' — which IS the slam poem
jokes.explanation: This is the best deployment of Perd's defining character trait — his pathological over-narration of the obvious — applied to an art form (slam poetry) that already borders on self-parody. The joke works on multiple levels: his announcement IS the poem, the meta-circularity is perfect, and it's completely organic to Perd. High originality, excellent structure, maximum economy. A genuinely brilliant character joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need to see the completed audition forms with all signatures and initials. Every single box checked. Every. Single. Box. Do you understand? I will literally not be able to sleep tonight if there's even one blank space. I'll just lie there, staring at the ceiling, thinking about that unchecked box. My eye will twitch. I'll start muttering to myself. By morning, I'll have reorganized my entire apartment by the Dewey Decimal System just to distract myself from the existential dread of administrative incompleteness.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben's talking head: 'I cannot tell the difference between what's supposed to be slam poetry and what's just him talking.'
jokes.setup: Perd has been performing his 'slam poem' which sounds identical to his normal narration
jokes.punchline: Leslie and Ben both can't distinguish his poem from regular speech — the meta-commentary landing perfectly
jokes.explanation: A strong callback that validates the joke setup in #3. The shared confusion between two normally composed people amplifies the absurdity. Efficient and well-placed.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: I am now reading poetry. I am holding a piece of paper. The paper has words on it. I am looking at the words. My eyes are moving from left to right. I am now moving my mouth. Sounds are coming out of my mouth. Some people are listening to the sounds. They are sitting in chairs. The chairs have legs. I am standing. My legs are also below me. I am wearing shoes on my feet.

jokes.text: Perd's second slam poem: 'My second slam poem is called "My Second Slam Poem by Perd Hapley," by Perd Hapley.'
jokes.setup: Perd announces he has a second slam poem
jokes.punchline: The title of the poem is as redundantly self-referential as everything else Perd says — the byline 'by Perd Hapley' is repeated twice
jokes.explanation: Escalates the Perd gag beautifully. The double attribution ('by Perd Hapley, by Perd Hapley') is the joke — pure Perd logic applied to titling. The escalation works because it deepens rather than just repeats the first beat.

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: I have prepared a poem for you all. It is called 'The Winds of Change.' The winds of change are blowing through our fair city. They bring with them the promise of tomorrow. And also some allergies.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: That's... that's just the news.

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: Yes. Yes, it is.

jokes.text: Leslie panicking about Andy potentially getting sick: 'Is that the Fred one or the Barney one?' (Andy about Vitamin C)
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Andy to take more Vitamin C; Andy says 'Copy that. Vitamin C.'
jokes.punchline: Andy sincerely asks whether Vitamin C is 'the Fred one or the Barney one' — revealing he confuses vitamins with Flintstones vitamins characters
jokes.explanation: Perfectly characterizes Andy's childlike ignorance — he thinks of vitamins as Flintstones characters. The non-sequitur lands because the logic is internally consistent with who Andy is. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: I'd like to read you my second poem. It's called 'Poem: A Poem About Poems.'

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: A poem, by Perd Hapley.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head about Pawnee being a breeding ground for disease: 'We used to crown Miss Influenza every year. The CDC called the pageant "ethically reprehensible."'
jokes.setup: Leslie explains that Pawnee has poor hygiene habits and high disease rates
jokes.punchline: The town held a Miss Influenza pageant — implying they celebrated flu infection — and the CDC condemned it
jokes.explanation: Sharp Pawnee worldbuilding joke. The specificity of 'ethically reprehensible' from the CDC is the right institutional voice to invoke. The image of crowning a flu queen is darkly absurd and very specific to Parks' universe of Pawnee being a comedically terrible town.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You should take vitamin C.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Vitamin C? Like, Vitamin Barney? Vitamin Wilma?

jokes.text: Leslie to quarantined Larry in a tent: 'The tent is your home now, Larry. We already forwarded your mail.'
jokes.setup: Larry says he doesn't feel well and asks to work from home
jokes.punchline: Leslie has already quarantined Larry in a tent outside and 'forwarded his mail' — implying permanent exile with bureaucratic efficiency
jokes.explanation: The 'forwarded your mail' line is the kicker — it implies Larry's banishment has been officiated with bureaucratic thoroughness. Classic Parks Larry joke with Leslie's obsessive task-orientation applied cruelly to poor Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And that's why we need to account for raccoon density in our flu prevention protocol. It's a well-documented vector.

jokes.text: Leslie recoiling from shaking hands after Chipp McCapp news: 'Wait, no, I don't want to touch your hand. Wow!'
jokes.setup: Ben excitedly announces he secured Chipp McCapp; Leslie starts to high-five/shake hands out of excitement
jokes.punchline: Mid-celebration, she remembers her flu paranoia and recoils — the excitement/horror whiplash
jokes.explanation: Functional running gag beat about Leslie's flu paranoia but not particularly inspired. The physical comedy of pulling back mid-handshake is a quick laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're throwing a pageant celebrating a disease that horrified health authorities across the country.

jokes.text: The Chipp McCapp fan nickname: 'We are huge Chippmunks. That's what his fans call themselves. I don't know why. Chippmunks. Because of the animal? No, that's too simple.'
jokes.setup: They're excited about teen country star Chipp McCapp and his fanbase
jokes.punchline: The fans are called Chippmunks — an obvious portmanteau of Chipp + chipmunks — but Leslie and Ben genuinely can't figure out the etymology, deciding it's 'too simple'
jokes.explanation: The joke is in their failure to process the obvious — 'No, that's too simple' is the best line. It satirizes fandom naming conventions while also characterizing Leslie and Ben as adults who overthink everything.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Larry, you can't work from home. You'll contaminate the office. I've set up a tent in the parking lot for you.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: A tent? Leslie, I have the flu, not leprosy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've also redirected all your mail there. It's safer this way.

jokes.text: Chipp McCapp's song 'Beautiful Like My Mom' — 'She don't care about no fancy trends / She's just a mom from old South Bend'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben describe Chipp McCapp as Indiana's sweetheart with 2 million YouTube hits
jokes.punchline: The song is aggressively wholesome/saccharine country — honoring mom from South Bend — delivered as if it's genuinely moving, while being objectively terrible
jokes.explanation: A competent parody of earnest teen country music. South Bend is the right specific detail. The joke is in the gap between how Leslie/Ben react (rapturous) and how objectively mediocre the song is.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why is the fan called 'The Breeze'? That's so obvious!

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Character
dialogue.line: It literally just blows air around.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, no. There's got to be something deeper. Some kind of hidden meaning or clever wordplay.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Character
dialogue.line: It's a fan. It makes a breeze.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Too simple. There's no way that's actually it.

jokes.text: Leslie/Ben listening to the song a second time: 'Let's play it again. Play it again.'
jokes.setup: The Chipp McCapp song has just played — it's saccharine and mediocre
jokes.punchline: Both of them are genuinely moved and want to hear it again, sincerely
jokes.explanation: The genuine sincerity of two intelligent adults being moved by this objectively corny song is the joke. The callback structure works — we've heard the song, we know it's silly, so their re-listen request lands.

dialogue.speaker: Chipp McCapp
dialogue.line: My dog ran away and my truck broke down, my wife left me in this one-horse town, I lost my job at the factory, now all I got is this bottle and me.

jokes.text: Tom announcing the wine country outing: 'Donna, April, wine country train is leaving the station. You ready?' and April's condition: 'if you drive us there, I will get very drunk.'
jokes.setup: Tom invites Donna and April to a sommelier competition at a vineyard
jokes.punchline: April's response reduces her entire participation to a simple transactional arrangement — driving in exchange for getting drunk
jokes.explanation: April's nihilistic transactionalism is perfectly in character. 'I will get very drunk' delivered as a deal term is funny because it's her most enthusiastic line.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, a sommelier is just a fancy word for a wine salesman. And salesmen? They're heroes. They're out there every day, grinding, hustling, making things happen. People don't respect sales enough. A sommelier walks into a room, suddenly everyone thinks he's sophisticated. That's the power of sales, baby. That's why I want to hire one.

jokes.text: Tom's confessional: 'People that convince other people to buy expensive stuff they don't need. Those are the real heroes.'
jokes.setup: Tom explains the sommelier competition — wine experts competing for certification
jokes.punchline: Tom's reverence for salesmanship as heroism is presented with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Pure Tom Haverford — his ethos reduced to a single crisp line. The 'real heroes' framing for luxury upsellers is pointed satire delivered through Tom's genuine belief.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know a lot about wine. I took a course in plant biology in college, and I went to Indiana University, so...

jokes.text: Ben says he studied botany for three years at Purdue ('Go Boilermakers!') as qualification to attend a wine event
jokes.setup: Tom didn't invite Ben; Ben is finding reasons to come to the winery
jokes.punchline: Ben's leap from 'I love wine' to 'I studied botany at Purdue' as credentials, capped with an unprompted college cheer, reveals his earnest but slightly off-base reasoning
jokes.explanation: Nice character beat for Ben — his nerd energy expressing itself through an unsolicited 'Go Boilermakers!' is very him. The logic that botany = wine expertise is endearingly misguided.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This wine trip is going to be amazing. Just me, some beautiful vineyards, and some of the finest wines in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, that sounds wonderful! Can I come?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, that does sound pretty cool.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm in.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Road trip!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No. No, no, no. This is not a group activity. This is a solo journey for a sophisticated man of culture and means.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Can I join?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh my God. No! Why would you... No!

jokes.text: The group that Tom didn't invite keeps joining: Ron, Ben, and others all 'tag along' to the vineyard, leaving Tom exasperated
jokes.setup: Tom intended a cool outing with just Donna and April
jokes.punchline: Ron announces he'll go ('There will be alcohol there'), then Ben, then more — each addition more deflating for Tom
jokes.explanation: Each addition is funny — Ron's 'There will be alcohol' as his sole criterion, the crowd ballooning despite Tom's protests. Good escalation structure.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. You're already embarrassing me and we haven't even started yet.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I started with two cool people and I ended up with a bunch of grandpas.'
jokes.setup: The entire office has invited themselves to Tom's wine outing
jokes.punchline: 'A bunch of grandpas' — Tom's verdict on Ron, Ben, etc.
jokes.explanation: Economical punchline. 'Grandpas' is the right specific insult from Tom's perspective — he values coolness above all else. Short and punchy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We could always call Dylan's people, see if any of his associates might want to headline.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: His associates? Leslie, Dylan's people are criminals and drug addicts.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, but they're very talented criminals and drug addicts.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Listen, grandpas. When we get to the vineyard, there'll be a lot of fancy people there. Please, I beg you, don't embarrass me.' Ben: 'How would we embarrass you?' Tom: 'You're already doing it. I begged you.'
jokes.setup: Tom preemptively begs the group not to embarrass him
jokes.punchline: Ben's sincere question 'how would we embarrass you?' is itself embarrassing — Tom points out the question alone proves his point
jokes.explanation: The recursive logic — asking how you'd embarrass someone is itself embarrassing — is sharp. 'I begged you' as a kicker is perfect comedic rhythm. Strong structure.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Character
dialogue.line: On-the-nose album title stating their position

jokes.text: Leslie's confessional: land Ho's lead singer titled their last album 'We'll Never Reunite'
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions Land Ho as a long-shot wish for the concert — 'But there's no way they're getting back together'
jokes.punchline: The album was literally titled 'We'll Never Reunite' — the band made their permanence explicit in the most unambiguous way possible
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the album title is inspired — it takes the 'band will never reunite' premise and literalizes it to absurd effect. Good setup for the later Land Ho payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Xander's got skills like Usher in the 2004 R&B landscape—smooth, precise, totally in command of his lane.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'There are no hands to be on deck because everybody's at the winery.'
jokes.setup: Chipp McCapp drops out; Leslie says 'all hands on deck'
jokes.punchline: She immediately realizes she sent everyone to a winery — undercutting her own command
jokes.explanation: Good structural irony — she invokes a team-effort cliché right after sending everyone away. The self-awareness landing well.

dialogue.line: Gross but probably real sommelier practice

jokes.text: Larry stumbles out of his quarantine tent and sneezes on Leslie right as she's trying to mobilize; she yells 'Damn it, Larry!'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been sneezed on and exposed to the flu she's been desperately avoiding
jokes.punchline: Larry emerges from his tent to sneeze directly on her — the visual of the quarantine tent and the resigned 'Damn it, Larry' is the payoff
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry joke — his very existence causes disaster. The tent setup pays off perfectly. 'Damn it, Larry' is a beloved Parks running gag and this is a solid deployment.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I want to join the competition so I can sabotage everyone else and watch them fail. It brings me joy.

jokes.text: Tom's confessional describing Xander: 'He's basically the Bruno Mars of Indiana amateur wine tasting.'
jokes.setup: Tom explains why Xander Truffant is his target hire
jokes.punchline: 'The Bruno Mars of Indiana amateur wine tasting' — an extremely over-specific superlative from a very narrow field
jokes.explanation: Tom's celebrity-comparison-as-compliment is his signature move, but the specificity of 'Indiana amateur wine tasting' as the domain makes this one land especially well. Very Tom, very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I went to the Culinary Institute of France for three years studying viticulture and oenology under the tutelage of the world's foremost wine experts. I also have a degree in French literature from the Sorbonne.

jokes.text: Xander explains he pours saline water through his nose to clear mucus from his 'smell centers'; Tom responds: 'That is the most beautiful thing I've ever heard.'
jokes.setup: Xander prepares for the tasting competition with an unusual ritual
jokes.punchline: Tom's reverential, sincere response to a disgusting nasal hygiene practice — he's so committed to finding Xander cool that everything Xander does becomes beautiful
jokes.explanation: The gap between the gross reality (saline nasal flush) and Tom's romantic response is the joke. Tom's sycophancy toward cool people he wants to impress is a consistent character trait deployed well here.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I belong here. I have a Roth IRA.

jokes.text: April at the sommelier competition: 'Oh, man. It costs $200 to get certified. I wanted to make fun of stupid people while I get drunk. My two true passions.'
jokes.setup: April finds out there's a certification fee to enter the competition
jokes.punchline: She summarizes her entire motivation as 'making fun of stupid people while getting drunk' — 'my two true passions' delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: Excellent April character joke. 'My two true passions' is perfectly deadpan and quotable. The self-awareness about her nihilistic motivations is peak April Ludgate.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I only drink alcohol that's clear or brown. I will not drink blueberry wine.

jokes.text: Tom offering to bankroll April's entry: 'You want to futz with these fools? I will bankroll you. Really? Oh, hell, yeah, pimp.'
jokes.setup: April can't afford the entry fee
jokes.punchline: Tom enthusiastically agrees to sponsor her specifically to 'futz with fools' — his language shifting to slightly anachronistic slang ('pimp') that feels off but very Tom
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat — Tom's impulse to be the cool benefactor. 'Pimp' as affirmation is a mild Tom-ism. Not exceptional but competent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Are you okay? Do you need medical attention?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm fine, I'm fine. Why does everyone keep asking me that?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because you have a giant bruise on your face.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, that's just from when I fell down the stairs at work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's terrible! We need to get you to a hospital.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm good. I'll just go punch myself a few more times. That usually helps.

jokes.text: April claiming to be from 'The Wine Academy' in Bordeaux; the sommelier immediately grants her entry to Group A based on the fake credential
jokes.setup: April is asked where she studied wine
jokes.punchline: She invents 'The Wine Academy' and immediately says it's 'in Bordeaux' when pressed — the official accepts it without question
jokes.explanation: The satire of credentialist gatekeeping is sharp — the official is so impressed by the vague prestige of 'Bordeaux' he skips all verification. April's flat delivery of obviously fake credentials is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need the strongest flu medicine you have. I have to be at a meeting tomorrow and I cannot miss it.

dialogue.speaker: Pharmacist
dialogue.line: This should do it, but you need to follow the instructions carefully.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Don't worry, I can handle it. I once organized an entire town festival while battling a stomach bug. I'm basically Mariah Carey.

dialogue.speaker: Pharmacist
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, a diva who demands perfection no matter what. Except instead of hitting high notes, I'm hitting deadlines.

jokes.text: Craig dramatically entering: 'I know I don't look the part, but I know everything about wine and I will prove it. My name is Craig Middlebrooks, and this is my debit rewards card.'
jokes.setup: Craig insists on joining the competition despite not being invited
jokes.punchline: His impassioned self-introduction climaxes in presenting his debit rewards card as if it's a credential — the deflation from dramatic declaration to mundane payment method
jokes.explanation: Craig's signature overblown dramatic energy applied to a completely ordinary situation. The debit rewards card as his calling card is a wonderful specificity. The structure is good — big buildup to mundane deflation.

dialogue.speaker: Pharmacist
dialogue.line: Well, let's see here. You've got a slight case of the sniffles.

dialogue.speaker: Pharmacist
dialogue.line: Actually, wait. That's pneumonia. You're going to die.

dialogue.speaker: Pharmacist
dialogue.line: Oh never mind, I wasn't looking at your chart. You're fine. That'll be fifteen dollars.

jokes.text: Ron tasting the blueberry wine: 'I don't drink alcohol from that portion of the color spectrum.'
jokes.setup: The vineyard offers blueberry wine; Ron is offered a glass
jokes.punchline: Ron refuses with a categorical principle — 'that portion of the color spectrum' — as if he has systematically mapped which colors of alcohol are acceptable
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Ron's rigid adherence to personal codes is perfectly deployed here — not just 'I don't like blueberry wine' but a systematic color-spectrum principle. The line is perfectly constructed, maximally economical, and completely specific to Ron Swanson's character. Highly quotable. Compares favorably to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, Leslie said I could buy two candies?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So if I buy one really huge candy, that counts as two, right? I'm gaming the system!

jokes.text: Ron, Craig, and Ben all immediately react to blueberry wine: 'Holy hell, that's a lot of alcohol.' — and they order four bottles
jokes.setup: Ron refused the wine; others tried it
jokes.punchline: Despite Ron's principled refusal, those who taste it are overwhelmed and immediately order four bottles — the strength of the wine overrides all pretension
jokes.explanation: Competent reaction beat. The group consensus of ordering four bottles after one sip is funny but the joke is more situational than crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Can I vent to you about something?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Of course. I'm going to have a drink, and when it's gone, this conversation is over.

jokes.text: Andy to Leslie: 'if you have to puke in my car, it's totally okay, I do it all the time.'
jokes.setup: Andy checks if Leslie is okay to travel despite feeling sick
jokes.punchline: Andy's casual admission that he regularly vomits in his own car is delivered as reassurance
jokes.explanation: Classic Andy — his attempt at reassurance only reveals more alarming information about his life. 'I do it all the time' as comfort is perfectly wrong-headed and specific to him.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: My mom called me again about my dad. They're having issues.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Ben, you need to stop letting them pull you into their drama.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know, but they're my parents. What am I supposed to do?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tell them to work it out themselves. You're a grown man.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ron, that's actually really good advice. You should be a therapist.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not. I have no interest in other people's problems.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Okay. Well, if you do collapse, luckily, I know first aid. Or karate. That's not first aid. It is if you do it right. Heimlich!'
jokes.setup: Andy is offering to help if Leslie gets worse on the road
jokes.punchline: Andy conflates karate with first aid, Leslie corrects him, and he doubles down — then demonstrates with 'Heimlich!' as if shouting it constitutes performing it
jokes.explanation: A strong Andy moment — the karate/first aid confusion is funny, but the Heimlich escalation ('It is if you do it right') is the best beat. Andy's internal logic is consistent and endearing. The sudden 'Heimlich!' is a great physical comedy button.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't take criticism well. But I'm working on it. In fact, I consider what you just said to be a genuine compliment, and I thank you for it.

jokes.text: Leslie at the pharmacy: 'I need the good stuff. The Mariah-needs-to-sing-tonight stuff.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is describing her flu symptoms to the pharmacist and asking for strong medicine
jokes.punchline: She invokes Mariah Carey as the reference standard for 'must perform regardless of illness' — implying she has a Mariah-level obligation
jokes.explanation: The Mariah Carey reference is specific and funny — invoking celebrity as shorthand for 'must-perform-regardless' is a clever observational move. Leslie comparing herself to Mariah is both grandiose and self-aware.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This wine tastes like if a Kardashian was a fruit.

jokes.text: New pharmacist diagnosing Leslie with 'aseptic meningitis — you have about an hour to live' then immediately walking it back: 'It's probably not that. Sorry, it's my first day.'
jokes.setup: Leslie describes her symptoms; the pharmacist says it doesn't look like the flu
jokes.punchline: He immediately suggests a fatal condition with an hour to live, then nonchalantly retracts it because it's his first day
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'doesn't look like flu' to 'hour to live' to 'it's my first day' is a tight structure with a great deflation. Dark but earned because the 'first day' explanation retroactively recontextualizes all his confident diagnoses.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I'm detecting notes of blackberry, oak, and a hint of vanilla.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Now I'm getting some leather, tobacco, and what appears to be a small child's scream.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Is that... is that the sound of a marriage ending? Yes, I'm definitely tasting a failed marriage.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: And underneath all that, I'm picking up notes of regret, broken dreams, and possibly a ghost.

jokes.text: Andy holding a candy and telling Leslie 'This counts as one.' — claiming one of his two candy allowances with a very specific candy choice implied
jokes.setup: Leslie allowed Andy two candies at the pharmacy
jokes.punchline: Andy is already managing his candy budget carefully — 'This counts as one' suggests he's strategizing his two-candy allocation
jokes.explanation: A small but charming Andy beat. The idea of a grown man carefully accounting his two-candy allowance is funny and endearing. Economical.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: This wine has notes of blackberry, hints of oak, a subtle undertone of tobacco with just a whisper of vanilla on the finish.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It tastes like wine.

jokes.text: Ron agreeing to let Craig vent: 'You may vent for as long as it takes me to drink this bottle of wine.'
jokes.setup: Craig asks 'Can I just vent for a sec?'
jokes.punchline: Ron's time limit for Craig's emotional disclosure is measured in wine consumption — implying he'll stop listening the moment his bottle is empty
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Ron lines. His contempt for emotional sharing is rendered through a perfectly calibrated practical measurement — not 'I'll listen for a minute' but 'as long as it takes me to drink this bottle.' The character integration is near-perfect: Ron, wine, and minimal emotional tolerance combined in one line. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: This wine has notes of... blackberry, and oak, and also my ex-girlfriend's betrayal.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: This one tastes like regret. Regret and... is that plum?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ooh, this one's got a real finish. It finishes with me crying in my car in the parking lot of a Home Depot.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: This wine pairs well with poor life choices and a complete lack of self-respect.

jokes.text: Ron's response after Craig says Ron is terrible to discuss personal problems with: 'Thank you, friend. That really means a lot to me.' — completely sincere
jokes.setup: Craig tells Ron he's a wonderful guy but terrible at discussing personal problems
jokes.punchline: Ron takes the 'terrible at personal problems' part as the compliment — genuine, warm gratitude
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect Ron character joke. He genuinely hears 'terrible at personal problems' as praise, because to him it IS praise. The sincerity of 'that really means a lot to me' is the kicker — zero irony, maximum character truth. This compares favorably to the 8.0 anchor in terms of character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie? Leslie, hi, it's me. It's Ben. Ben Wyatt. I'm a man. I have a face. I work at the government. I'm calling you on a phone.

jokes.text: April's wine tasting description: 'It's mostly pumpkin. There's so much pumpkin, it's like a Charlie Brown Halloween special.'
jokes.setup: April is performing a wine tasting description at the competition
jokes.punchline: She describes the pumpkin note not with wine-expert vocabulary but with a specific pop culture comparison to Charlie Brown Halloween
jokes.explanation: The 'Charlie Brown Halloween special' reference is inspired — it's culturally specific, evocative, and completely out of place in a sommelier competition, which is exactly right for April. The image lands vividly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm calling to tell you that waffles are just pancakes that decided to get their life together. And also, I think Ben doesn't know that I reorganized his entire sock drawer by thread count.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Did you know that the word 'government' has 'govern' in it? Like, that's not a coincidence. Someone planned that. That person is a genius.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Anyway, I'm going to go eat a entire wheel of cheese and call it dinner. Love you. Bye!

jokes.text: April's wine notes: 'I'm getting notes of dried robin's blood, old dirty cashews from your grandfather's basement, and just a hint of a robot's bathwater.'
jokes.setup: April continues her sommelier tasting description
jokes.punchline: She rattles off increasingly absurd flavor notes in perfect sommelier cadence — 'robot's bathwater' as the kicker
jokes.explanation: This is the funniest joke in the episode. The escalating absurdity — dried robin's blood → old dirty cashews from grandfather's basement → robot's bathwater — is perfectly constructed, each note more absurd than the last while maintaining the cadence of real wine-speak. 'Robot's bathwater' is an exceptional piece of comic writing: it's specific, visual, absurd, and somehow feels like it almost makes sense as a flavor note. Highly quotable, high rewatch value. This is the episode's standout joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: My phone just died. It's like when Stanley Kubrick died.

jokes.text: Craig's wine descriptions escalating to 'This comes from your mother's butt. Possibly your father's butt.' then correcting himself: 'This comes from John McEnroe's butt from the year 3055.'
jokes.setup: Craig is competing in the sommelier tasting — he's been trying to identify wines
jokes.punchline: He pivots from trying to identify the wine to a series of increasingly unhinged 'butt' attributions — first the judges' parents, then a self-correction to John McEnroe's butt from the year 3055
jokes.explanation: Craig's volcanic personality finds its perfect expression in a wine competition where social norms demand restraint. The 'butt' escalation is well-constructed — 'your mother's butt' is already unhinged, 'possibly your father's' self-corrects to MORE unhinged, and 'John McEnroe's butt from the year 3055' is a spectacular non-sequitur. The year 3055 detail is the genius touch.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'll walk you home.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh, thanks Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's this way.

jokes.text: Leslie emerges from bathroom: 'Man, you were in the bathroom forever.' — then immediately pivots to normal conversation
jokes.setup: Leslie is nauseous with the flu while they wait for Chipp McCapp
jokes.punchline: Andy's mild 'forever' understates what was clearly a significant illness episode, and the immediate pivot to cheerful normalcy is the joke
jokes.explanation: Functional beat. The reaction suggests Leslie has been sick in the bathroom for a long time; Andy's casual understatement and pivot are character-appropriate but not exceptional comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm dating a baseball player.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, I'm not actually dating him, but I told everyone at the wine thing that I was.

jokes.text: Andy has made all the coffee pods in the hotel lobby: 'Check it out, I made all the little coffee pods they had.'
jokes.setup: Leslie went to the bathroom while waiting for Chipp; Andy was left alone in the lobby
jokes.punchline: Andy has industriously brewed every single coffee pod in the hotel lobby presumably into a collection of cups, displayed with pride
jokes.explanation: Perfectly characterizes Andy's childlike inability to be idle — presented with pods, he made them all. The visual of a table full of tiny coffee cups is the implied comedy. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, 'je ne sais quoi'? Really, Terrence? You don't know what? It's literally the name of the thing you're describing. That's not French, that's just giving up.

jokes.text: Craig's lake house story: his parents couldn't decide who gets the dog, so they dropped it off at a synagogue.
jokes.setup: Craig is venting about his parents' petty conflicts over their shared property
jokes.punchline: The escalating examples of parental dysfunction reach 'dropped the dog off at a synagogue' — an absurdly specific resolution that raises more questions than it answers
jokes.explanation: Strong absurdist detail. The specificity of 'local synagogue' — rather than generic 'shelter' or 'neighbor' — is what elevates this from a generic bad-parents joke. Craig's 'I was, like, Say what?' is a funny reaction that shows he too finds this logic bewildering.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: For a nice steak, you want a wine with some backbone. Something assertive, confident, maybe a little neurotic and self-deprecating. So basically, a wine that's like a humor writer.

jokes.text: Leslie's garbled phone call to Ben: 'It's your me. It's wife. It's Leslie. Knope.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is sick and trying to call Ben with big news
jokes.punchline: The flu has degraded her communication to near-incomprehensible fragments — 'It's your me. It's wife.' — she can't even string together 'it's your wife'
jokes.explanation: The comedy of Leslie Knope — the most competent person in the room — being reduced to 'It's your me. It's wife.' by illness is effective. The word order collapse is funny and specific.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: This wine has notes of blackberry, plum, and a hint of... is that... blood? Yeah, this tastes like evidence from a murder scene.

jokes.text: Ron reacting to Ben's phone update: 'Oh. Phone water.' — describing Leslie's incoherence
jokes.setup: Ben is confused by Leslie's garbled call about 'blue teeth' and a dog
jokes.punchline: Ron's entire diagnosis of the situation is 'Phone water' — two words, perfectly deadpan
jokes.explanation: Ron's two-word diagnosis is maximally economical. He correctly identifies the problem (Leslie is drunk/sick) with minimum words. Perfect Ron delivery beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chipp
dialogue.line: I need my sandwiches cut diagonally, not straight across. And the bread has to be toasted to exactly 347 degrees. The lettuce must be arranged in a counter-clockwise pattern, and each piece of cheese needs to be individually blessed by a spiritual healer before it touches the bread.

jokes.text: Ben: 'It's as dead as Stanley Kubrick.' — describing his dead phone
jokes.setup: Ben's phone dies mid-call with Leslie
jokes.punchline: He describes it as 'dead as Stanley Kubrick' — a random celebrity death reference used as a simile for phone battery
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing as a random specific reference but not particularly well-crafted. Stanley Kubrick is an odd choice that doesn't add much beyond randomness. Medium laugh.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Thank you. I want to say that wine is just old juice and anyone who pretends to like it is a liar. The 'notes' you taste are made up. That 'full body' you're experiencing is just expensive marketing. I'm going to use my platform as sommelier champion to tell people the truth: wine is bad and we should all just drink beer or vodka like normal people.

jokes.text: Ben, watching Ron walk away: 'Also, if I leave you alone, I'm pretty sure you'll die.'
jokes.setup: Ben says he doesn't want to wait for Tom and wants to walk home; Ron says he'll join
jokes.punchline: Ron's secondary reason for joining Ben is that he believes Ben will literally die without supervision — delivered with complete casual sincerity
jokes.explanation: Ron's paternalistic affection for his friends disguised as a survival assessment. The casualness of 'I'm pretty sure you'll die' as a matter-of-fact observation is classic Ron.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I want to thank Eddie Murphy's worst movies for inspiring me to be better.

jokes.text: Donna: 'You know I picked up a little French-Canadian when I dated that Montreal Expo.'
jokes.setup: Tom notices a suspicious fancy competitor speaking French
jokes.punchline: Donna casually mentions she learned French-Canadian from dating a Montreal Expo — implying she dated a baseball player while also just casually knowing obscure French-Canadian
jokes.explanation: The Montreal Expo detail is perfect Donna — her romantic history with athletes is a running character element, and the Expos (a defunct team) are an oddly specific choice that makes it funnier. Classic Donna confidence and backstory.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm gonna outbid him. How much is he offering?

dialogue.speaker: Xander
dialogue.line: Twelve thousand dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm out.

jokes.text: Tom vs. Terrence: 'That was my idea.' 'That is everyone's idea. That is why we have this, how do you say, thing.' Tom: 'Okay, don't act like you don't know the word "thing."'
jokes.setup: Tom meets French restaurateur Terrence Montreaux who owns 12 restaurants and is also scouting sommeliers
jokes.punchline: Terrence's affectation of not knowing English words ('how do you say, thing') is punctured by Tom pointing out 'thing' is too basic a word to not know
jokes.explanation: The 'how do you say' affectation is a familiar French stereotype, but Tom's specific puncturing of it ('don't act like you don't know the word thing') is the sharp specific beat that elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Character
dialogue.line: I'm out of alcohol. It's like my bottle broke its promises to me.

jokes.text: April recommending wine pairing: 'With a filet mignon, I'd recommend a red. Something bold and dry, like David Sedaris.'
jokes.setup: April is performing sommelier recommendations
jokes.punchline: She describes a wine as 'bold and dry, like David Sedaris' — invoking the author as a wine quality descriptor
jokes.explanation: Genuinely inspired. 'Bold and dry, like David Sedaris' works as an actual wine description (his writing IS bold and dry) while being completely absurd in context. The reference is specific enough to reward recognition and absurd enough to work even without it. One of the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I don't know what you want from me.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: A man is what he does, not what he says he'll do.

jokes.text: Craig responding to the red wine with steak suggestion: 'Not if you're eating steak, you loon.'
jokes.setup: The judge suggests a Riesling with the filet mignon instead of a red
jokes.punchline: Craig breaks sommelier decorum to call the judge a 'loon' for suggesting white wine with steak
jokes.explanation: 'You loon' is a funny word choice — slightly archaic insult that's specific to Craig's overblown register. The intemperance in a formal setting is classic Craig.

dialogue.speaker: Chipp
dialogue.line: Casually insulting his own fanbase

jokes.text: April's wine description: 'You know in the movies, when the cops show up and find lipstick on a wine glass next to a dead body? This is that wine.'
jokes.setup: April continues her unorthodox sommelier descriptions
jokes.punchline: She describes a wine by its association with a murder scene — 'this is that wine' — invoking a crime drama cliché as a flavor note
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The crime scene wine description is April at her best — dark, specific, and perfectly structured. 'This is that wine' as the payoff is economical and punchy. The visual evocation is vivid and unexpected. Strong originality and character integration. Compares favorably to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Chipp
dialogue.line: I want to shoot the gun!

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.line: No, you're too young.

dialogue.speaker: Chipp
dialogue.line: But I WANT to! You're the worst father ever!

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.line: Fine, here's the gun.

dialogue.speaker: Chipp
dialogue.line: I'm gonna shoot you!

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.line: That's my boy!

jokes.text: Chipp McCapp's behind-the-scenes behavior: 'Can somebody give me one of those LunchStacks? And stack them for me this time. Cheese on top, or no one gets paid.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Andy have just met Chipp McCapp, who seemed wholesome and grateful to fans
jokes.punchline: Immediately after his fans leave, he barks entitled demands — specifically 'cheese on top, or no one gets paid' for his lunch
jokes.explanation: Good subversion of the wholesome teen star persona. 'Cheese on top, or no one gets paid' is a specific and petty demand that effectively reveals his true character. The contrast between his fan-facing warmth and immediate backstage entitlement is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, Chipp, you think you're so smart? Well, I'm going to get you back for this.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh no, not again. Last week she spent three hours planning an elaborate prank involving a fake permit application.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's because it works, Andy!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, but she does this like every other day. I've already had to create a spreadsheet to track her revenge plots.

jokes.text: Chipp's dad brings the wrong sandwich — turkey instead of ham. Chipp: 'You dick.'
jokes.setup: The dad/manager brings the LunchStack sandwich with cheese on top of turkey
jokes.punchline: Chipp calls his father 'you dick' over a sandwich — revealing the depths of his entitlement and the dad's submissive enabling
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe beat. The shock of a teenager calling his father 'you dick' to his face is the joke, and the father's non-reaction (just picking up the food) deepens it. Sets up Leslie's moral objection.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, Leslie, I know you're worried about how your family's gonna handle you moving up in your career. But trust me, big families adapt. My family's huge and we figure it out.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's really sweet, Andy. I'm actually pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: See? Your family's gonna be so excited when you tell them you got a promotion!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, Andy. I'm pregnant. With a baby.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Right, yeah, and that's gonna be great for your career trajectory. You're gonna crush it.

jokes.text: Dad's response to the ham complaint: 'They were out of ham.' / Chipp: 'All right, well, maybe I should just let Mom be manager, then?' / Dad: 'Pick them up, Skipp.' (Presumably telling his other son to help)
jokes.setup: Chipp threatens to replace his dad as manager
jokes.punchline: The dad's response is to redirect to a task — 'Pick them up, Skipp' — a rhyming command that reveals there's another son named Skipp, which is its own bizarre detail
jokes.explanation: Secondary cringe beat. The 'Skipp' rhyme with 'Chipp' is a small but genuine absurdist detail — this family has children named Chipp and Skipp. Functional continuation of the bit, not especially strong on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so the baby's gonna be inside Ann the whole time? Like, living in there?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's incredible. So basically Ann's a spaceship now. She's literally carrying precious cargo.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Does the baby need, like, a seatbelt in there? Because that seems like a safety issue.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! I know what we should do. We should talk to the baby every day so it knows our voices. I read that somewhere, or I'm pretty sure I did.

jokes.text: April wins the sommelier competition and announces: 'I think we can agree that all wine tastes the same. And if you spend more than $5 on wine, you are very stupid.'
jokes.setup: April has just been announced the winner of the sommelier competition
jokes.punchline: In her victory speech, she reveals she has learned nothing and holds the entire discipline in contempt — puncturing the whole event with anti-elitist nihilism
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke — she wins the competition by demonstrating the most complete contempt for what it's testing. The victory speech as a denunciation of the field is perfectly April. 'You are very stupid' is the right blunt kicker.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Blueberry wine. A bold choice. Most people don't understand the complexity of berry fermentation. The ancient Mesopotamians believed blueberries contained the tears of forgotten gods. Personally, I just appreciate that it pairs well with venison and solitude.

jokes.text: April's thank-you speech invoking Norbit, Pluto Nash, 'all the Klumps'
jokes.setup: April continues her acceptance speech after winning the sommelier competition
jokes.punchline: She thanks Eddie Murphy movies — specifically Norbit, Pluto Nash, and 'all the Klumps' — as her inspirations
jokes.explanation: The specificity of thanking Eddie Murphy's critically maligned movies (Norbit, Pluto Nash) rather than his acclaimed work is a nice April-specific touch. She'd specifically choose the 'bad' ones. The 'all the Klumps' adding the plural is the right escalation beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ron, I'm assigning you to play an emotion.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Leslie, emotions are a sign of weakness. I don't have them.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: You're playing Anger.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I'm not angry.

jokes.text: Tom to Xander: 'Look. Tom's Bistro is going to be the dopest, quite possibly trillest restaurant in the area.'
jokes.setup: Tom pitches Xander to work at Tom's Bistro
jokes.punchline: 'Quite possibly trillest' — Tom's pitch for his restaurant maxes out at 'the trillest in the area' as a superlative, which is both overstated and oddly qualified
jokes.explanation: Tom's slang ('trillest') as a business pitch term is funny. 'Quite possibly' as a hedge on 'trillest' undercuts the sales pitch in a way that's accidentally honest and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I'm not getting that job. I can feel it. And you know what? I'm fine with it. I'm going to go home, I'm going to get a bottle of the cheapest scotch they have, I'm going to pour it into a glass that still has yesterday's lipstick on it, I'm going to get into bed, I'm going to scroll through pictures of my ex-girlfriend's vacation, and I'm going to cry until my eyes are swollen shut.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I'll double whatever he's paying you.' Xander: 'You'll pay me $500,000 a year?' Tom: 'I will pay you one-tenth of whatever he's paying you.'
jokes.setup: Tom offers to double Terrence's offer; Xander reveals the number is $500,000
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately recalculates to one-tenth — not $1,000,000 but the inverse — a complete capitulation while trying to maintain dignity
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The math reversal — from 'double' to 'one-tenth' — is both perfectly timed and brutally deflating. The joke structure is tight: setup (Tom's bravado), turn (the $500K reveal), punchline (one-tenth). Tom's hustle crashing against reality is one of the show's recurring pleasures and this is a sharp example.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Dunn
dialogue.line: What if we did some role-play therapy? You embody anger, and I'll try to talk you down.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Fine. I'm angry.

jokes.text: Ron and Ben encounter the Eagleton Ron Dunn appearing from nowhere in the dark: 'Whoa! Where'd you come from? Uh, that's a complicated question. All depends on whether your conception of time is linear or circular.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Ben are walking home from the vineyard
jokes.punchline: Ron Dunn materializes from nowhere and responds to the practical question 'where did you come from?' with a philosophical answer about linear vs. circular time
jokes.explanation: Ron Dunn's New-Age philosophical character is well-deployed here — the literal question 'where'd you come from?' answered with time philosophy is a sharp character contrast to Ron Swanson's pragmatism. 'Linear or circular' is the right specific phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I will tone it down. I will be LESS INTENSE. I will speak in a measured, calm, and reasonable manner AT ALL TIMES. I WILL NOT RAISE MY VOICE. I WILL NOT USE EXCESSIVE PUNCTUATION OR DRAMATIC GESTURES. I WILL SIT QUIETLY AND THINK PEACEFUL THOUGHTS. I WILL MEDITATE ON THE NATURE OF TRANQUILITY AND ZEN-LIKE CALM. NAMASTE.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Dude. Are you a ghost?' Ron Dunn: 'Am I?'
jokes.setup: Ron Dunn has appeared mysteriously in the dark
jokes.punchline: His response to 'are you a ghost?' is to turn it back as a genuine question — 'Am I?' — not denying it, just philosophically uncertain
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — two words that perfectly capture Ron Dunn's New Age mysticism. Not denying being a ghost is funnier than any denial would be. The character integration is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You just gotta tell him that his academic success was actually an accident. Like, he didn't mean to get good grades, it just happened.

jokes.text: Chipp's dad Skipp: 'They do buy a lot of albums.' Then immediately: 'They sure ain't buying toothpaste. Bunch of dirty hicks.'
jokes.setup: Andy and Leslie argue that Pawnee needs Chipp for the Unity Concert — that it serves the whole region
jokes.punchline: Skipp briefly advocates for Pawnee (album sales), then undercuts it with a contemptuous dig about toothpaste and 'dirty hicks'
jokes.explanation: The pivot from endorsement to insult is well-timed. 'They sure ain't buying toothpaste' is a funny specific detail and 'bunch of dirty hicks' as an afterthought lands well. Plays on the established Pawnee-as-terrible-town running theme.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Karate! Hi-YAH! Karate! Hi-YAH!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's time to learn karate, it's time to learn karate, it's time to learn karate from me!

jokes.text: Chipp: 'If I want to shoot a paintball gun at my dad, I'm going to do it.' — then does it; Skipp: 'Good shot, son. I'm proud of you.'
jokes.setup: Chipp is defending his right to do whatever he wants
jokes.punchline: He uses 'shooting my dad with a paintball gun' as his example of freedom — then does it on the spot; Skipp's approving response ('Good shot, son. I'm proud of you.') makes it more absurd
jokes.explanation: The best Chipp/Skipp joke. The entitlement manifesting as literal violence on his own father, AND the father's congratulatory response, reveals the depth of the dysfunction. 'Good shot, son. I'm proud of you.' is the kicker that elevates it from simple slapstick to dark character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I'm going to deliberately give you wrong wine pairings to see how you react.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Wait, what?

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: For a fish course, I'm recommending this heavy Cabernet Sauvignon.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: That's... that's completely wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: And for dessert, a dry, tannic Barolo.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Who are you?

jokes.text: Leslie's parting shot: 'you should know that, when you shook my hand earlier, there was pee on my palms.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Chipp Pawnee doesn't need him and they're leaving
jokes.punchline: She deploys a final gross-out revelation — pee palms — as a parting humiliation
jokes.explanation: Funny because it's Leslie — ordinarily so dignified and professional — deploying a juvenile gross-out tactic as her exit. The flu degrading her professionalism is a running theme that pays off here.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, so Craig could hear everything we were saying in that office?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, the walls are basically paper thin.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, no. Last week I was in there telling Ben about my entire business plan for Rent-A-Swag.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Your what now?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Exactly! Craig heard it first!

jokes.text: Andy: 'You get pee-palm, too? Every time!'
jokes.setup: Leslie announces she had pee on her palms during the handshake
jokes.punchline: Andy reveals he also got pee palm AND this apparently happens to him regularly ('Every time!') — with the exasperation of someone who keeps getting pee on their hands
jokes.explanation: 'Every time!' is the perfect escalation — Andy has a pattern of pee palm incidents. The comedic implication of a life where pee palms are a recurring problem is absurd and specific to Andy's disaster-magnet character.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I don't believe in spirit animals. That's not based in any kind of science or logic.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: My spirit animal is the bald eagle.

jokes.text: Andy's SAT strategy: 'Same way I got a perfect score on the SATs. Broken Scantron machine.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks how they'll convince Scott Tanner to reunite Land Ho
jokes.punchline: Andy reveals his SAT perfect score came from a broken Scantron — not academic excellence but mechanical failure
jokes.explanation: Sharp Andy joke — the specificity of 'broken Scantron machine' rather than just cheating makes it funnier. It implies Andy didn't even cheat actively; the machine just failed in his favor. Perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going home to tell Ben some big news.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh my god, you're getting a dog! That's so exciting! You're gonna love it. Pro tip: get the biggest bag of dog food you can find. It lasts way longer, and dogs don't care about freshness.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, I'm not getting a dog.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, you'll change your mind. Everyone does. Also, name it something cool like Thunderbolt or Rape Ape.

jokes.text: Tom, very drunk, mishears 'doggy bag' as 'she's gettin' a dog!' and announces it to the restaurant
jokes.setup: April asks the waitress for a doggy bag; Tom is drunk
jokes.punchline: Tom's blurred hearing/comprehension turns 'doggy bag' into Leslie's pregnancy-dog misunderstanding — also a callback to Andy's dog confusion
jokes.explanation: A nice callback to the dog confusion running through the episode — the theme of 'getting a dog' being misunderstood resurfaces here with Tom's drunkenness as the mechanism. Not exceptional but structurally satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: You are like a caterpillar in a cocoon. And soon, you will emerge as a beautiful butterfly and spread your wings and fly away... from government.

jokes.text: Ron Dunn proposes a role-play: 'Let's role-play. I'll be your father. And, Ron, you take the role of Ben's anger.'
jokes.setup: Ron Dunn is trying to help Ben process his anger about his parents selling the lake house
jokes.punchline: Ron Dunn assigns Swanson the role of 'Ben's anger' — an abstract emotion — as if it's a normal acting exercise
jokes.explanation: The casting of Ron Swanson as 'Ben's anger' — personifying an emotion — is a nice absurdist touch. Ron's presumably disgusted reaction to this assignment is implied.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, so that didn't work at all.

jokes.text: Craig's exit monologue: 'I'm going to go home and feel totally fine. Who am I kidding? I'm going to go home, put on a Macy Gray album, and cry in the mirror!'
jokes.setup: The vineyard day is ending; Craig is disappointed he didn't get the Tom's Bistro job
jokes.punchline: Craig's over-sharing about his emotional breakdown plans — specifically 'Macy Gray album' and 'cry in the mirror' — is delivered with theatrical self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Craig's self-aware dramatic vulnerability is perfectly deployed. 'Macy Gray album' is the right specific choice — obscure enough to be funny, nostalgic enough to land. 'Cry in the mirror' as the specific act is very Craig. The pivot from 'totally fine' to full breakdown in one sentence is classic Craig escalation.

jokes.text: Craig reveals he wanted the Tom's Bistro sommelier job all along: 'Are you all blind? I want that job at Tom's Bistro. I've been trying to show you for the last five hours.'
jokes.setup: Tom and the group assumed Craig was just participating for fun
jokes.punchline: Craig has had a genuine professional goal all day that no one noticed because his personality made it incomprehensible
jokes.explanation: A good structural reveal. Craig has been sincerely competing while everyone thought it was chaos. The joke is that his legitimate professional goals are indistinguishable from his unhinged behavior. Retroactively funny on rewatch.

jokes.text: Tom's response to Craig wanting the job: 'You're like a crazy volcano. You'd have to show me you can bring it down a notch.' Craig: 'I'll bring it down 1,000 notches if I have to!'
jokes.setup: Tom says Craig is too volatile to hire despite his skills
jokes.punchline: Craig's response to 'bring it down a notch' is to promise to bring it down 1,000 notches — delivered at maximum Craig-volume, proving Tom's point
jokes.explanation: Excellent self-defeating joke. Craig loudly promising to calm down — the very act of promising confirming he can't — is structurally perfect. '1,000 notches' as his hyperbolic counter is precisely the wrong response delivered with perfect character truth. The irony is built into the structure: the punchline proves the premise. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Andy's Karate Chop Master performance at Scott Tanner's house — singing a children's song to a rock legend to convince him to reunite his band
jokes.setup: Andy and Leslie are trying to convince rock legend Scott Tanner to reunite Land Ho; the approach is failing
jokes.punchline: Andy breaks into his Johnny Karate children's performer routine — a karate-themed singalong — to connect with Tanner's kid, which unexpectedly gets Tanner to sing along
jokes.explanation: The joke is Andy using a children's karate song to do serious diplomatic work with a rock legend. The absurdism of the tactic and the fact that it WORKS is the payoff. The repeated failed attempts to get Scott in on the harmony ('No. No. It's not... You didn't...') extends the gag effectively.

jokes.text: Craig, as sommelier at Tom's Bistro (test/audition): serving a customer who orders 'full-bodied red with fish' and ice cubes in wine — 'I'll have a glass of your most expensive red wine mixed with a glass of your cheapest white wine, served in a dog bowl. And silly straws all around.'
jokes.setup: Craig is being tested as a potential sommelier by Tom, April, and Donna who order increasingly wrong wine pairings
jokes.punchline: The orders escalate from merely wrong (red with fish) to bizarre (ice cubes in red wine) to theatrical sabotage (expensive red + cheap white in a dog bowl with silly straws)
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the terrible orders is well-constructed. 'Dog bowl and silly straws' is the right peak absurdity. The test structure creates good tension for Craig's reaction.

jokes.text: Craig's internal monologue (to himself in the conference room that has no sound privacy): 'What kind of monster orders red with fish? I know they're messing with me and it's just a test, but have some decency!'
jokes.setup: Craig goes to 'compose himself' in a back room, not knowing it's an open conference room everyone can hear
jokes.punchline: His private meltdown is fully audible — and specifically 'have some decency!' as his outburst confirms he hasn't brought it down at all
jokes.explanation: The joke works as a callback to Craig's promise to calm down — his 'private' composure-gathering moment still involves audible outrage about decency. The soundless conference room reveal adds a nice ironic layer.

jokes.text: Craig eavesdropping revelation: 'Can you hear everything people say in that conference room? I've been taking what I thought were private phone calls. I've heard everything. I know all about the car dealership in Tampa.'
jokes.setup: Tom realizes Craig can hear everything from the conference room
jokes.punchline: Craig has been inadvertently accumulating damaging secrets — specifically 'the car dealership in Tampa' — and uses it as an implicit threat
jokes.explanation: The 'car dealership in Tampa' is the right specific detail — mysterious enough to be funny, specific enough to imply actual wrongdoing. Craig accidentally leveraging secrets to get the job is a funny dark turn.

jokes.text: Ron Dunn's fire ceremony: 'You're surrendering to the Earth Mother. Now, stare into the fire and picture your spirit animal.' Ron Swanson: 'I don't know what my spirit animal is. Because it doesn't exist because that's nonsense because you're an adult.'
jokes.setup: Ron Dunn has set up a fire ceremony to help Ben and Ron process their emotions
jokes.punchline: Swanson's triple-because rejection of the spirit animal concept — 'because it doesn't exist because that's nonsense because you're an adult' — is a stacked logical dismissal
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top Ron Swanson jokes. The triple-stacked 'because' structure is a beautifully constructed dismissal — each clause adds another layer of exasperation. 'Because you're an adult' as the final kicker implies the whole premise is a category error. Highly quotable and character-perfect.

jokes.text: Ben's spirit animal is a baby snow owl. Ron Dunn: 'He's right.' — completely serious
jokes.setup: Ron Dunn asks everyone to picture their spirit animal; Ron Swanson has rejected this
jokes.punchline: Ben sincerely identifies 'baby snow owl' as his spirit animal; Ron Dunn validates this with complete authority
jokes.explanation: Ben's unselfconscious sincerity ('baby snow owl') is right for his character — he's secretly earnest. Ron Dunn's immediate validation ('He's right') is the perfect absurdist confirmation.

jokes.text: Ron Dunn urging Ben to burn the check in the fire; Ron Swanson: 'Do not burn that check. It is money.' Ron Dunn: 'No. Ron is right, Ron.'
jokes.setup: Ron Dunn says Ben should burn his share of the lake house proceeds to release anger
jokes.punchline: Ron Swanson's objection is pure pragmatism ('It is money'); Ron Dunn then agrees and addresses 'Ron is right, Ron' — the two Rons in agreement is absurd
jokes.explanation: 'Do not burn that check. It is money.' is peak Ron Swanson — pure distilled pragmatism in one sentence. 'Ron is right, Ron' creates a charming absurdity of two Rons agreeing. High character integration for both.

jokes.text: Andy confesses: 'Especially since I threw up in that guy's piano.'
jokes.setup: Andy and Leslie celebrate the Land Ho news — Leslie says Andy 'really saved the day'
jokes.punchline: Andy quietly reveals he vomited in Scott Tanner's piano at some point — delivered as an afterthought that recontextualizes the entire victory
jokes.explanation: Excellent delayed reveal joke. The off-hand delivery of 'I threw up in that guy's piano' is the key — it arrives after the victory moment and lands as a pure Andy disaster detail. The piano is a specific enough detail to be very funny. High rewatch value — knowing this happened during the earlier scene adds to it.

jokes.text: Andy's continued confusion about Leslie's pregnancy: 'Now you need to get home. You and Ben have some planning to do... You're gonna need a cage, a water bowl. You have a good vet? Tick medicine.'
jokes.setup: Leslie confirms she's pregnant; Andy is ostensibly giving advice
jokes.punchline: Andy still thinks she's getting a dog — his advice is entirely dog-specific — 'cage, water bowl, tick medicine'
jokes.explanation: A nice extended callback to the dog misunderstanding. 'Tick medicine' as his parting pregnancy advice is the right escalating specific detail. Andy sustaining the misunderstanding is funny.

jokes.text: Ron Dunn's car runs on vegetable oil and bat guano: 'Actually cleans the air as it drives.'
jokes.setup: Ron Swanson declines a ride from Ron Dunn
jokes.punchline: Ron Dunn's car runs on bat guano — a sufficiently disgusting fuel — but he insists it 'actually cleans the air as it drives,' a scientifically dubious claim
jokes.explanation: Ron Dunn's eco-mysticism extending to his vehicle is a good character beat. 'Bat guano' is the right specific disgusting detail. The 'cleans the air' claim is appropriately absurd.

jokes.text: Ron Dunn's inspirational speech about Ben 'emerging from his cocoon' and 'will you fly?' — followed by Ben bluntly: 'Yeah, I don't feel any better. I'm still angry. Damn it.'
jokes.setup: Ron Dunn delivers a beautiful, sweeping speech about Ben's spiritual journey and transformation
jokes.punchline: Ben's immediate verdict is flat disappointment — the entire New Age ceremony had zero effect
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the entire Ron Dunn B-plot: the elaborate ceremony accomplished nothing. Ben's 'Damn it' puncturing all the mysticism is a satisfying deflation. The delay before Ben speaks makes the deadpan land harder.

jokes.text: Ron Dunn apologizing: 'Sorry we couldn't help you work through your problems. Now, if you'll excuse me, I've got a lady, two little girls, and an infant waiting for me. It's always nice to see the kids at the end of a long day. Really puts things in perspective.'
jokes.setup: Ron Dunn has failed to help Ben process his anger about his parents selling his childhood home
jokes.punchline: Ron Dunn immediately pivots to how he goes home to his warm family — implicitly demonstrating the very perspective-giving experience Ben is denied regarding family memories
jokes.explanation: The irony is gentle — Ron Dunn unknowingly rubs Ben's family wound with his own family contentment. Moderately effective character moment but not a strong joke per se.

jokes.text: Ben's tearful resolution about the lake house: 'I want to start our family. I mean, I know things are crazy, but there's no good time. And I want to do it. Now.' Leslie: 'Well, buddy, I've got some good news for you.'
jokes.setup: Ben has just had an emotional breakthrough — he wants to start a family with Leslie
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response of 'I've got some good news for you' confirms she's been pregnant the whole episode — the ultimate callback/payoff to the episode's mystery
jokes.explanation: The emotional and comedic capstone of the episode. Ben articulating his desire for a family in the same episode where Leslie is pregnant creates a satisfying structural echo. 'I've got some good news for you' lands both as comedy and as warm emotional payoff. The timing is excellent.

tmdb_overview: Leslie and Ben run a charity auction to raise funds for the unity concert. April steps in to manage Andy's schedule, while Donna asks Ron for help with her ex-boyfriend.
insight: Absurdist escalation carries 67 jokes through a mid-tier flu episode despite weak standouts.
